societies.name: Fractale — the connected provision system
societies.society: Human participants receiving the network’s material benefits

scope.period: Established functioning coverage before the Temple’s final crisis and reboot
exclusions: The post-reboot order as already identical

societies.description:
Fractale supplies sustenance, medical care and basic income in return for personal data. Everyday survival is therefore separated from an ordinary job: the network provides a continuing floor while residents lead largely individualized lives. The guarantee estimate is strong inside functioning coverage, but it is not unlimited. Relays fail, people outside coverage lose the system’s benefits, and even the administrators have difficulty maintaining the inherited infrastructure. This scope precedes the final reboot rather than assuming it solves every access problem.

The Temple administers the order through priestly institutions and force. That supports concentrated human control rather than broad ownership by every connected resident. Calling the system a god or using holographic avatars does not itself establish an autonomous AI sovereign. A high nonworking estimate follows the explicit freedom from necessary employment and the generally leisurely way of life, with a wide allowance for useful study, care, maintenance and voluntary creation. It is a rough editorial estimate, not a canonical census, and avatars do not multiply the population.

guarantees.basis: Real food, care and income provision exists within coverage, but failures and uncovered refugees qualify security.

control.basis: Temple institutions administer and enforce the system; personal network use does not establish shared productive ownership.

nonworking.basis: The system explicitly removes necessary employment and supports leisure; the broad noncanonical range allows substantial chosen useful work.

evidence.claim: The network supplies sustenance, medical care and basic income, while failed coverage produces excluded refugees.

uncertainties: Coverage-limited ordinary floor rather than universal unbroken access.
The Temple’s ultimate repair capacity is limited.
The participation point is explicitly approximate.
Doppels and physical people are not counted twice.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages, including explicit uncertainty; no independent reviewer

societies.name: Fractale — Granitz’s off-grid Lost Millennium community
societies.society: The Granitz faction’s rejection of automatic network provision

scope.period: The established Granitz community before the final Temple attack
scope.population: Living members of the Granitz faction
exclusions: Other Lost Millennium factions as identical

societies.description:
Granitz’s community rejects a readily available network that would supply material support, choosing independence, embodied interaction and practical work instead. It is retained as an interpretive zero variant: useful human effort returns because people deliberately avoid an automatic support arrangement. Preserving jobs is not their stated primary aim, so that difference from a formal employment quota remains explicit. The community still uses advanced tools and aircraft; its policy is selective rejection of dependence rather than a total absence of technology.

Authority belongs to human community members and their leaders. A positive control estimate reflects local practical autonomy, while leaving uncertainty about legal ownership and the influence of military leadership. The sources do not establish an unconditional welfare floor within the faction, so guarantees stay unresolved. Hard work is valued and continues, but no reliable participation census is supplied. The broader Lost Millennium umbrella includes factions with different methods, and their actions are not assigned automatically to Granitz. The later teaching of independent life does not establish an identical worldwide economy.

guarantees.basis: Rejection of network benefits is clear; internal entitlement, needs coverage and exclusions are not fully described.

control.basis: Local human self-direction contrasts with Temple dependence, but communal ownership and leadership constraints are incompletely specified.

nonworking.basis: Valued manual/practical work is not a census of all members’ useful activity.

evidence.claim: Traditionalists reject the system’s provided benefits and organize around practical work and independence.
evidence.locator: Anime Herald traditionalist-work account and Granitz faction description

uncertainties: The zero label is interpretive and disputed: autonomy rather than job creation motivates the rejection.
Only the Granitz faction is scoped.
Selective off-grid practice is not a universal ban on technology.
Internal guarantee and participation axes remain unresolved.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages, including explicit uncertainty; no independent reviewer

societies.name: Eden — Sara’s hidden robot-supported upbringing
societies.society: The living child raised by agricultural robots outside Eden 3

scope.period: Sara’s continuing childhood before the final general-awakening resolution
scope.population: Sara, the living human child in the hidden household

societies.description:
Two agricultural robots raise Sara after finding her in stasis, sustaining a living human child in a continuing hidden household. The productive robot community grows food, and the child’s care is not purchased through her current wages or supplied by an ordinary human family workforce. This is a deliberately tiny automatic-support unit, rather than a claim that all preserved humans are awake and enjoying leisure. Its material-guarantee estimate is moderately strong but broad because safety depends on secrecy outside the main settlement.

The providers are autonomous robots after their former human masters have disappeared. Their affection and willingness to care do not make Sara their owner, so control lies toward independent machine provision. That differs from saying every robot shares the same hostile policy or that the household itself is tyrannical. Sara learns and can undertake useful activity, and the checked summaries do not support a precise nonworking percentage. The sleeping population remains outside the active-person denominator. The ending’s wider awakening is a different prospective community whose durable allocation rules are not established here.

guarantees.basis: Continuing agricultural provision and care are real, but clandestine residence and uncertain wider protection qualify security.

control.basis: The independent robot caregivers provide resources without a current human owner; benevolence is distinct from human productive control.

nonworking.basis: A child’s learning/help may be useful activity; neither age nor stasis gives an exact participation rate.

evidence.claim: Farming robots secretly raise an awakened living human child in a safe haven.
evidence.locator: Netflix synopsis and continuing agricultural/upbringing description

uncertainties: A single living human support unit, not all frozen humans.
The discovery embryo wording is not used as a verified population description.
Autonomous caring providers are distinct from human-owned appliances.
The final general awakening is not a second established welfare regime.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages, including explicit uncertainty; no independent reviewer

decisions.follow_up: Keep the short gap/comparison and continue without whole-series or novel reconstruction.

decisions.reason: Atlas’s privileged shelter and financial technology do not establish a post-work material-access constitution.
decisions.analysis: Carbon trading and urban exclusion are not sufficient evidence of labor replacement or a free support floor.
decisions.follow_up: Keep the short gap/comparison and continue without whole-series or novel reconstruction.

decisions.reason: Clear references establish sustenance, care and income supplied by the functioning network.
The Granitz community deliberately rejects available automatic provision in favor of independent practical life; the interpretive limitation is explicit.
A living child has actual continuing agricultural-robot support, separately from sleeping humanity.

review_notes: Previous goal turn was progress: 448/110 to 520/117. Continue from authoritative saved state, not the old objective checkpoint.
Twelve fast decisions and three records, including one explicitly interpretive technological-opt-out zero variant.
Fractale official Japanese episode descriptions support benefit dependence and coverage refugees. The short review establishes material support directly; no full series was read/viewed.
Sara is a living child, not a multiplied population of sleeping humans. Biological human-derived Queerats and psychic human work are not robots.
Unrelated company welfare, carbon-hotel reports, software orchestrators and historical Lost Millennium hits were discarded.
